title: Static Electricity: Sparks All Around
summary: How rubbing moves tiny charged bits called electrons, why charged things pull or push, why dry air brings more shocks, and how lightning is a giant spark.
poll: Static electricity is more useful than it is annoying.

versions.title: Zap!
versions.text:
You walk on a rug. You touch a door. Zap! You feel a small shock. What was that?

All things are made of tiny bits. Some of the bits have a charge. You can not see them.

When you rub two things, some bits move. They go from one thing to the next. Now each thing has a charge. This is static.

Rub a balloon on your hair. Now hold it up to a wall. It sticks! Things with charges that are not the same attract. That means they pull close.

Your hair may stand up, too. Each hair has the same charge. So they push apart.

Dry air makes more shocks. Wet air lets the charge leak out. In Riyadh, the air is dry. So zaps are a lot more common there.

A spark is charge that jumps. Lightning is a huge spark. It jumps from a storm cloud.

So the next time you feel a zap, you will know why!

versions.title: Zap! A Tiny Spark
versions.text:
You walk on a soft rug. Then you touch a metal door. Zap! You feel a quick shock. What just happened?

Everything is made of tiny bits. You can not see them. Some of these bits have a charge.

When you rub two things together, some tiny bits move. They jump from one thing to the other. Now both things have a charge. We call this static.

Try this. Rub a balloon on your hair. Then hold it up to a wall. It sticks! Things with different charges attract. That means they pull toward each other.

Your hair may stand up, too. Each hair now has the same charge. Things with the same charge push away. So the hairs spread apart.

Dry air makes more shocks. Wet air helps the charge leak away. Riyadh has very dry air. So people there often feel little zaps.

A spark is charge that jumps across the air. Lightning is a giant spark. It jumps from a storm cloud.

Next time you feel a zap, you will know the reason!

versions.title: Static Electricity: Tiny Sparks
versions.text:
You walk across a soft carpet. Then you reach for a metal door handle. Zap! You feel a quick sting. What made that tiny shock?

Everything around you is made of tiny bits. They are much too small to see. Some of these bits carry an electric charge.

When you rub two things together, some of the tiny bits move. They jump from one thing to the other. Now both things have a charge. This is called static electricity.

Here is a test. Rub a balloon on your hair. Then hold it next to a wall. It sticks! Things with different charges attract. That means they pull toward each other.

Look in a mirror, too. Your hair may stand up! Each hair now has the same kind of charge. Things with the same charge push away from each other. So the hairs spread apart.

Dry air makes more shocks. Wet air helps the charge leak away slowly. Riyadh has very dry air, so people there often feel little zaps.

A spark is a charge that jumps through the air. Lightning is a giant spark that jumps from a storm cloud.

So the next time you feel a zap, you will know why it happened!

versions.title: Static Electricity: Tiny Sparks
versions.text:
You shuffle across a soft carpet and reach for a metal door handle. Zap! A quick sting jumps to your finger. What caused that tiny shock?

Everything around you is made of tiny bits that are far too small to see. Some of these bits carry an electric charge. Most of the time, the charges in an object are balanced.

When you rub two things together, some of the tiny charged bits move from one object to the other. Now each object has a charge. This is called static electricity, because the charge stays in one place until it can escape.

Try a simple test. Rub a balloon on your hair, then hold it next to a wall. It sticks! Objects with different charges attract, which means they pull toward each other.

Now look in a mirror. Your hair may be standing up! Every hair has the same kind of charge, and things with the same charge push away from each other. So the hairs spread apart.

Dry air makes static shocks more common. Wet air helps the charge leak away slowly. Riyadh has very dry air, so people there often feel little zaps, especially in winter.

A spark is a charge jumping through the air. Lightning is a giant spark that leaps from a storm cloud.

So the next time you feel a zap, you will know exactly why!

versions.title: Static Electricity: Sparks All Around
versions.text:
You shuffle across a carpet in your socks and reach for a metal door handle. Zap! A tiny spark jumps to your finger, and you feel a quick sting. That surprise has a simple cause.

Everything is made of atoms, which are far too small to see. Atoms contain even tinier particles. Some of these particles, called electrons, carry a negative electric charge, while other particles carry a positive charge. Usually the charges in an object are balanced.

When two materials rub together, some electrons can move from one material to the other. One object ends up with extra electrons, and the other object has too few. Both objects now have a charge. This is called static electricity, because the charge stays still until it finds a way to escape.

Try rubbing a balloon on your hair and holding it near a wall. The balloon sticks! Opposite charges attract, which means they pull toward each other.

Your hair may stand on end, too. Each hair now has the same charge, and like charges repel, or push each other away. That is why the hairs spread apart.

Dry air makes static shocks more common. In humid air, a thin layer of water lets the charges leak away. Riyadh has very dry air, so people there often feel small shocks, especially in winter.

A spark is electricity jumping across the air. Lightning is a giant spark that leaps from a storm cloud.

versions.text:
Imagine shuffling across a carpet in your socks and then reaching for a metal door handle. Zap! A tiny spark jumps to your finger, and you feel a sudden sting. That surprising moment has a clear scientific explanation.

Everything is made of atoms, which are far too small to see. Atoms contain even tinier particles. Electrons carry a negative electric charge, while other particles in the center of the atom carry a positive charge. Usually the positive and negative charges in an object are balanced.

When two materials rub together, some electrons can move from one material to the other. One object then has extra electrons, and the other object has too few. Both objects become charged. Scientists call this static electricity, because the charge stays in place until it finds a way to escape.

Rub a balloon on your hair and hold it near a wall, and the balloon will stick. That happens because opposite charges attract, which means they pull toward each other.

Your hair may also stand on end. Each hair now carries the same type of charge, and like charges repel, or push each other away. As a result, the hairs spread apart.

Dry air makes static shocks more common. In humid air, a thin film of water on surfaces helps charges leak away gradually. Riyadh has extremely dry air, so residents frequently feel small shocks, especially during the winter months.

A spark is electricity jumping across a gap of air. Lightning is simply a gigantic spark that leaps from a storm cloud.

versions.title: Static Electricity: Sparks All Around
versions.text:
Imagine shuffling across a carpet in your socks and then reaching for a metal door handle. Zap! A tiny spark leaps to your fingertip, and you feel a sudden sting. That surprising moment has a scientific explanation that begins with particles far too small to observe.

All matter is composed of atoms, and atoms contain even tinier particles. Electrons carry a negative electric charge, while particles in the nucleus, the center of each atom, carry a positive charge. Ordinarily the positive and negative charges in an object are balanced, so the object has no overall charge.

When two different materials rub together, some electrons can travel from one material to the other. One object then possesses extra electrons, while the other is left with too few, so both become electrically charged. Scientists call this static electricity, because the charge remains stationary until it discovers a path to escape.

If you rub a balloon against your hair and hold it near a wall, the balloon will cling there, because opposite charges attract, meaning they pull toward each other.

Your hair may also stand on end. Each strand now carries the same type of charge, and since like charges repel, or push each other away, the strands spread apart.

Dry air makes static shocks considerably more common. In humid air, a thin film of moisture on surfaces allows charges to leak away gradually. Riyadh has extremely dry air, so residents frequently notice small shocks, particularly during winter.

A spark is electricity jumping across a gap of air, and lightning is simply a gigantic spark that leaps from a storm cloud, where tiny pieces of ice collide and build up enormous charges.

People noticed static long ago. More than 2,500 years ago, observers in ancient Greece discovered that amber, a hardened tree resin, could attract bits of straw after being rubbed with fur. The word electricity actually comes from elektron, the Greek name for amber.

versions.title: Static Electricity: The Science of Sparks
versions.text:
Imagine shuffling across a carpet in your socks and then reaching for a metal door handle. Zap! A tiny spark leaps to your fingertip, producing a sudden sting. That surprising moment has a precise scientific explanation, which begins with particles far too small to observe.

All matter is composed of atoms, and every atom contains even smaller particles. Protons, located in the nucleus at the center of the atom, carry a positive electric charge, while electrons, which move around the nucleus, carry a negative charge. Ordinarily the protons and electrons in an object are equal in number, so the object is neutral, possessing no overall charge.

When two different materials rub together, some electrons can transfer from one material to the other. One object then possesses extra electrons and becomes negatively charged, while the other, left with too few, becomes positively charged. Scientists call this static electricity, because the charge remains stationary until it discovers a path to escape.

If you rub a balloon against your hair and hold it near a wall, the balloon will cling there, because opposite charges attract each other with a force that is strong enough to overcome the balloon's light weight.

Your hair may also stand on end. Each strand now carries the same type of charge, and since like charges repel, or push one another away, the strands separate.

Dry air makes static shocks considerably more common. When humidity is high, a thin film of moisture on surfaces allows charges to leak away gradually. Riyadh has extremely dry air, so residents frequently experience small shocks, particularly during winter, when indoor heating and air conditioning remove additional moisture.

A spark is electricity jumping across a gap of air, and lightning is essentially a gigantic spark discharged from a storm cloud, where countless ice particles collide and gradually separate enormous quantities of charge.

Humans noticed this phenomenon long ago. More than 2,500 years ago, observers in ancient Greece discovered that amber, a hardened tree resin, could attract bits of straw after being rubbed with fur, and the word electricity actually comes from elektron, the Greek name for amber.

Ordinarily the protons and electrons in an object are equal in number, so the object is electrically neutral, possessing no overall charge.

When two different materials rub together, some electrons can transfer from one material to the other. One object consequently possesses surplus electrons and becomes negatively charged, while the other, left with a deficiency, becomes positively charged. Scientists describe this phenomenon as static electricity, because the accumulated charge remains stationary until it discovers an available path to escape.

If you rub a balloon vigorously against your hair and hold it near a wall, the balloon will cling there, because opposite charges attract each other with a force that is sufficiently powerful to overcome the balloon's modest weight.

Your hair may also stand on end. Each strand now carries an identical type of charge, and since like charges repel, or push one another away, the individual strands separate dramatically.

Humans recognized this phenomenon centuries before anyone understood it. More than 2,500 years ago, observers in ancient Greece discovered that amber, a hardened tree resin, could attract fragments of straw after being rubbed with fur, and the word electricity actually derives from elektron, the Greek name for amber.

keyWords.example: Rub your hands together to warm them up.
A magnet can attract a paper clip.

keyWords.definition: a tiny flash of light that jumps quickly
keyWords.example: We saw a spark fly up from the campfire.

keyWords.definition: a big bright flash in the sky during a storm
keyWords.example: We counted the seconds between the lightning and the thunder.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to build a storm cloud
Why balloons float up high and stay up in the air
What static is and why it makes zaps and sparks
How to stay dry in the rain
questions.why: The article explains how rubbing gives things a charge, how charges pull or push, and why we feel zaps and see sparks.

wrong.A: Storm clouds are mentioned, but the article does not tell how to build one.
wrong.B: A balloon sticks to a wall, but the article is not about floating.
wrong.D: Rain is not the topic of the article.

options: Some tiny bits move from one thing to the other
Both things get very cold
The two things turn into water
Both things lose all of their color and turn gray

wrong.C: Nothing turns into water in the article.
wrong.D: The article says nothing about color.

questions.stem: Why does a rubbed balloon stick to a wall?
options: The balloon is wet
Things with charges that are not the same pull close
The wall has glue on it
Things with the same charge push apart

wrong.C: There is no glue. Static makes the balloon stick.
wrong.D: Same charges push apart, so that would not make the balloon stick.

questions.stem: Why does your hair stand up after you rub a balloon on it?
options: Each hair gets wet
The hairs get much too hot from all of the rubbing

Each hair has the same charge, so they push apart

wrong.A: The hair does not get wet.
wrong.B: Heat is not the reason given in the article.
wrong.C: The article does not talk about wind.

questions.stem: In the article, the word attract means to —
options: push away
pull close
jump across
break apart
questions.why: The article says things with charges that are not the same attract, which means they pull close.

wrong.A: Push away is the opposite of attract.
wrong.C: A spark jumps across, but that is not what attract means.
wrong.D: Break apart is not what attract means.

People in Riyadh touch a lot more doors every day

wrong.B: The article never says people in Riyadh touch more doors.
wrong.D: The article does not say Riyadh has more storms.

questions.stem: How is lightning like the zap you feel from a door?

Both happen only at night

Both are made of rain

wrong.B: The article does not say either one happens only at night.
wrong.C: Lightning comes from a storm cloud, not a balloon.
wrong.D: Neither one is made of rain.

LOW.prompt: Tell what happens when you rub a balloon on your hair. Use the words charge and attract.
checklist: I told what rubbing does to the tiny bits.

MID.prompt: Explain why a rubbed balloon sticks to a wall but two rubbed hairs push apart. Use attract and repel.
checklist: I explained how rubbing moves electrons.
I used attract and repel correctly.
I used details from the article as evidence.
MID.modelAnswer: When I rub a balloon on my hair, electrons move from my hair to the balloon, so the balloon ends up with extra electrons and my hair has too few. The balloon and the wall have different charges, so they attract and the balloon sticks. But two hairs that lost electrons both have the same charge, so they repel and push apart from each other.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how a spark from a door handle and a bolt of lightning are related. Use the words electron and discharge.
checklist: I explained how charge builds up in each case.
I explained what a spark is and how lightning compares.
I supported my answer with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: In both cases, charge builds up because electrons move from one object to another until the objects are no longer neutral. When I shuffle across a carpet, extra electrons collect on my body, and when I touch a metal door handle, those electrons rush across the air in a sudden discharge that we feel as a spark. Lightning works the same way, but on a massive scale: a storm cloud builds up a huge imbalance of charge until it discharges as a giant spark between the cloud and the ground. The article also notes that dry air, with low humidity, makes these sparks more common because there is no moisture to let the charge leak away slowly.
